tips.title: If there is an à, you turn
tips.body: **tout droit** is *straight on*; **à droite** is *right*. One letter apart, opposite instructions. The **à** is the tell: *à droite* and *à gauche* are turns, *tout droit* is not.

tips.title: The vous imperative is free
tips.body: Take the *vous* form of the present and **drop the word *vous***. *vous tournez* → **Tournez**. Nothing else changes — unlike the *tu* imperative of an *-er* verb, which loses its **s**.

tips.title: Write down the number
tips.body: *Première*, *deuxième* and *troisième* differ only in the first syllable and come fast, and the ordinal is the detail most often missed in listening. If you note one thing while listening, note the number.

tips.title: Opposite is across the road
tips.body: **en face de** = opposite, across the road. **à côté de** = next to, beside it on the same side. A map question can be answered wrongly on this alone, so listen for *face* or for *côté*.

tips.title: Verb, number, direction, landmark
tips.body: *Prenez la deuxième rue à droite après les feux.* Keep that order and you never have to work out word order — and it matches the order the instruction will be given to you in.

steps.title: Demander son chemin
steps.body:
Asking the way needs one phrase, and there are two that always work.

- **Pardon, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?** — Excuse me, where is the station, please?
- **Pour aller à la gare, s'il vous plaît ?** — How do I get to the station, please?

The second is the more natural one and the one you will hear. Literally it is *to go to the station?* — French leaves the rest unsaid.

Two more that are worth having:

- **Est-ce qu'il y a une banque près d'ici ?** — Is there a bank near here?
- **C'est loin ?** — Is it far?

**Watch the article after *à*.** *Pour aller* **au** *cinéma* (masculine), *pour aller* **à la** *gare* (feminine), *pour aller* **à l'** *hôpital* (vowel), *pour aller* **aux** *magasins* (plural). It is the same *au / à la / à l' / aux* pattern as everywhere else.

And begin with **pardon** or **excusez-moi**. It costs one word and it is the difference between asking and demanding.

steps.title: Tout droit ou à droite ?
steps.body:
These two phrases differ by **one letter** and mean completely different things. Getting them the wrong way round sends you somewhere else entirely, and it is the commonest error in the topic.

$$\textbf{tout droit} = \textbf{straight on} \qquad \textbf{à droite} = \textbf{right}$$

The way to keep them apart:

- **tout droit** has **tout** in it — *all*, as in *all the way along*. Straight on.
- **à droite** has **à** — *to the* right. A turn.

So if there is an **à**, you are turning. If it starts with **tout**, you are not.

The third is easy: **à gauche** — left. It matches *à droite* in shape, which is a small help: the two turns look alike, and the one that is not a turn looks different.


And a useful extra: **la deuxième rue à droite** — the second street on the right. The direction word goes at the **end**.

steps.title: L'impératif avec vous
steps.body:
Directions are given as **instructions**, so they use the **imperative**. Because you are asking a stranger, it is the **vous** imperative — and that form could hardly be simpler:

$$\textbf{Take the vous form of the present tense and drop the word vous.}$$

- *vous tournez* → **Tournez** — turn
- *vous allez* → **Allez** — go
- *vous prenez* → **Prenez** — take
- *vous continuez* → **Continuez** — carry on
- *vous traversez* → **Traversez** — cross

Nothing else changes. No ending is removed, no accent shifts.

That is worth stating clearly because the **tu** imperative of an *-er* verb **does** change — *tu tournes* → *tourne*, dropping the **s**. The *vous* form has no such exception, and directions from a stranger are always *vous*.

**In use:**

- *Allez tout droit.* — Go straight on.
- *Tournez à gauche aux feux.* — Turn left at the lights.
- *Prenez la deuxième rue à droite.* — Take the second street on the right.
- *Continuez jusqu'au carrefour.* — Carry on as far as the crossroads.
- *Traversez le pont.* — Cross the bridge.

steps.title: Où exactement ? Les prépositions
steps.body: Once you have arrived in the right street, the **preposition** says exactly where the place is. These are what the question usually turns on. - **en face de** — opposite - **à côté de** — next to - **entre … et …** — between … and … - **devant** — in front of - **derrière** — behind - **près de** — near - **loin de** — far from - **au coin de** — on the corner of **The ones ending in *de* contract**, exactly as you would expect: - *en face **du** cinéma* (de + le) - *en face **de la** gare* - *en face de l'église* - *en face **des** magasins* (de + les) *Devant* and *derrière* take **no** *de* at all: *devant la gare*, *derrière l'école*. **The pair to be careful with** is *en face de* and *à côté de*. **Opposite** means across the road facing it; **next to** means beside it, on the same side. A listening question that hinges on which one it was is asking whether you heard three syllables or four — so listen for *face* and for *côté*.

steps.title: À toi : donne le chemin
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Traduis en français :

1. Go straight on.
2. Turn left.
3. Take the first street on the right.
4. It's opposite the station.

**Partie B.** Écris les directions :

5. From the square: straight on, then second right. The post office is next to the bank.
6. From the station: cross the bridge, carry on as far as the traffic lights, turn left.

**Partie C.**

7. Écris une question pour demander le chemin à la piscine, puis une autre pour demander si c'est loin.
8. *Prenez la troisième rue à droite, et le musée est entre la mairie et la poste.* Où est le musée, exactement ?

For question 1, check you have written *tout droit* and not *à droite*. They differ by one letter and send you in different directions.

steps.title: Aller plus loin : écouter les détails
steps.body:
**The one-letter trap, once more.** *Tout droit* is **straight on**; *à droite* is **right**. In a listening exam they sound quite different — *too drwah* against *ah drwat* — but on paper, under pressure, they are one letter apart. If there is an **à**, you are turning.

**Four details, any of which could be the question.** A direction like *prenez la deuxième rue à gauche, c'est en face de l'église* contains:

- the **verb** — take, not cross
- the **number** — second, not first
- the **direction** — left, not right
- the **preposition** — opposite, not next to

A listening question will pick **one** of them. So do not listen for the gist: listen for which street, which side, and which preposition. The gist is the same in every one of these questions.

**Numbers are the most missed.** *Première*, *deuxième*, *troisième* differ only in their first syllable, and they come fast. If you are going to write anything down while listening, write the number.

**En face de against à côté de.** Both put the building near the other one, and both are four or five syllables. But **opposite** is across the road and **next to** is beside. A map question can be answered wrongly on this alone, so listen for *face* or for *côté* rather than for the shape of the phrase.

**Giving directions: the order is fixed.** *Verb, then distance or number, then direction, then landmark.* *Prenez la deuxième rue à droite après les feux.* Sticking to that order means you never have to think about word order, and it matches how the instruction will be said to you.

**Two phrases worth having for when it goes wrong.** *Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?* and *Je n'ai pas compris.* In a speaking exam asking someone to repeat is not a failure — it keeps the exchange going, and the exchange is what is being marked.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- Ask with **Pour aller à…, s'il vous plaît ?** or **Où est…, s'il vous plaît ?**
- Start with **pardon** or **excusez-moi**.
- **tout droit** = **straight on**. **à droite** = **right**. **à gauche** = **left**.
- If there is an **à**, you are turning; if it starts with **tout**, you are not.
- The **vous imperative** is the **vous form of the present with *vous* dropped**: *tournez, allez, prenez, continuez, traversez*. Nothing else changes.
- The **tu** imperative of an *-er* verb loses its **s** — but directions from a stranger are always **vous**.
- **la première / deuxième / troisième rue à droite** — the direction goes at the **end**.
- **en face de** = opposite (across the road). **à côté de** = next to (beside it).
- Prepositions ending in *de* contract: **du, de la, de l', des**.
- **devant** and **derrière** take no *de*.
- In a listening question the answer turns on **one** of four details: the verb, the number, the direction, or the preposition.
- **Numbers are the most missed** — if you write anything down, write the number.
- Giving directions, keep the order: **verb, number, direction, landmark**.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Une réponse complète :**

*Pour aller à la piscine, sortez de la gare et **allez tout droit**. **Puis prenez la deuxième rue à gauche**. Continuez jusqu'au pont et **traversez le pont**. La piscine est **en face de l'école**.*

**Ce qui compte ici :**

- **Allez tout droit**, not *à droite* — the one-letter trap.
- **La deuxième** rue, not the first. The number is a mark of its own.
- **À gauche** — the direction goes at the **end**, after the street.
- **Traversez** — the *vous* imperative, the present *vous* form with *vous* dropped.
- **En face de** l'école — *opposite*, not *à côté de*, which would be beside it.
- **Puis** joins the instructions, so it reads as a route rather than a list.

**Pour aller plus loin :** *Ce n'est pas très loin, c'est à peu près cinq minutes à pied* adds distance, and *si vous arrivez au carrefour, vous êtes allé trop loin* adds a landmark to check against — both sound like real directions rather than an exercise.

questions.prompt: Explique la différence entre *tout droit* et *à droite*, et explique pourquoi il faut écouter les détails et non le sens général quand on entend des directions.
questions.solution: Tout droit veut dire straight on en anglais, tandis que à droite veut dire right. Les deux expressions ne diffèrent que d'une lettre à l'écrit, mais elles indiquent des directions complètement différentes, et c'est pour cette raison que c'est l'erreur la plus fréquente dans ce sujet. Une façon de les distinguer est de remarquer que s'il y a un à, on tourne, tandis que tout droit commence par tout, qui veut dire all, comme si on continuait tout le long de la rue. Quand on écoute des directions, il faut faire attention aux détails plutôt qu'au sens général, parce que le sens général est toujours le même : quelqu'un explique comment aller quelque part. Ce qui change, et ce sur quoi porte la question, c'est l'un des quatre détails : le verbe, par exemple prenez ou traversez, le numéro de la rue, par exemple la première ou la deuxième, la direction, à droite, à gauche ou tout droit, et enfin la préposition, par exemple en face de, qui veut dire de l'autre côté de la rue, ou à côté de, qui veut dire juste à côté. Les numéros sont les plus souvent manqués parce que première, deuxième et troisième ne diffèrent que par la première syllabe.

questions.modelAnswer:
**La différence.** *Tout droit* = **straight on**. *À droite* = **right**. They differ by one letter in writing but send you in completely different directions, which is why it is the commonest error in this topic.

**Comment les distinguer.** If there is an **à**, you are **turning**. *Tout droit* begins with *tout* — *all* — as in all the way along.

**Pourquoi écouter les détails.** The **gist is always the same**: someone is explaining how to get somewhere. What changes — and what the question is about — is **one of four details**:

- the **verb**: *prenez* or *traversez*
- the **number**: *première* or *deuxième*
- the **direction**: *à droite*, *à gauche*, *tout droit*
- the **preposition**: *en face de* (across the road) or *à côté de* (beside it)

**Le détail le plus souvent manqué** is the **number**. *Première*, *deuxième* and *troisième* differ only in the first syllable and come fast — so if you write anything down while listening, write the number.

examTechnique.body:
Check every time whether you mean tout droit or à droite. They are one letter apart and opposite instructions.

Form the vous imperative by dropping the word vous from the present tense form, and change nothing else.

Put the direction at the end: la deuxième rue à droite.

When listening, follow one instruction at a time and note the number, which is the detail most often missed.

Decide whether you heard en face de or à côté de. Opposite is across the road; next to is beside it.

In a speaking exam, ask someone to repeat rather than guessing. The exchange is what is marked.
examinerErrors: Writing à droite for straight on, or tout droit for right.
Missing the ordinal, so taking the first street instead of the second.
Confusing en face de with à côté de.
Writing en face de le cinéma instead of en face du cinéma.
Adding de after devant or derrière.
Using the tu imperative when giving directions to a stranger.
Putting the direction before the street, as in à droite la deuxième rue.
Listening for the gist rather than for the detail the question asks about.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never confuses *tout droit* with *à droite*, because it has a rule rather than a memory: the **à** means a turn. It forms the *vous* imperative instantly and knows why the *tu* form of an *-er* verb is different. Listening, it follows one instruction at a time and notes the ordinal, knowing that the gist of every such question is identical and the answer always turns on one small detail. And when giving directions it keeps to verb, number, direction, landmark, which makes the route easy to follow and the word order automatic.
